steps.body: Four terms, no common factor overall? **Group in pairs.** x³ + 3x² + 2x + 6: the first pair shares x², the second shares 2 — x²(x + 3) + 2(x + 3). Now both pieces share the binomial **(x + 3)**: pull it out to get **(x + 3)(x² + 2)**.

widget.prompt: Group x³ + 5x² + 4x + 20 as x²(x + 5) + 4(x + 5). What comes next?

options.label: pull out (x + 5): (x + 5)(x² + 4)
options.feedback: Right — the shared binomial factors out like any common factor.

options.label: add the groups: x² + 4 + 2(x + 5)
options.feedback: The groups are TERMS of a sum sharing (x + 5) — factor it out, don't merge them.

options.label: pull out x²: x²(x + 5 + 4)
options.feedback: Only the first group carries x² — the SHARED factor is the binomial (x + 5).

options.label: stop — it's fully factored
options.feedback: x²(x + 5) + 4(x + 5) is still a SUM — factoring means writing it as a product: (x + 5)(x² + 4).

steps.body: Check the leftover piece. x² + 2 = 0 would need x² = −2 — its zeros are the complex pair **±i√2**, so it contributes **no real zeros**. The only real zero of (x + 3)(x² + 2) is **−3**: a cubic whose graph crosses the axis exactly once.

explanationVariants: (x + 3) dies at −3; x² + 2 needs x² = −2 — complex only. One real zero.
The quadratic factor's discriminant is 0 − 8 < 0: no real contribution.

options.feedback: The pairs share (x − 2): x²(x − 2) and +5(x − 2) — signs come from the grouping.

options.feedback: The second group is +5x − 10 = +5(x − 2) — the 5 is positive.

options.label: x²(x − 2) + 5x − 10
options.feedback: Finish the job: 5x − 10 = 5(x − 2), and then the binomial factors out.

explanationVariants: Grouping works only when both pairs reveal the SAME binomial — that's the checkpoint.
Different binomials means regroup or try another method.

widget.prompt: After grouping, you get x²(x + 4) + 3(x + 2). What does this tell you?

options.label: the grouping failed
options.feedback: Right — (x + 4) ≠ (x + 2): no shared factor to pull. Regroup or change method.

options.label: pull out both binomials
options.feedback: You can only factor out a factor COMMON to both terms — these binomials differ.

options.label: the polynomial is prime
options.feedback: A failed grouping isn't proof of primeness — other arrangements or methods may still work.

options.label: add the binomials: (2x + 6)
options.feedback: Binomials in separate products don't add — the mismatched pair just means this grouping fails.

explanationVariants: (x + 3)(x² + 2) = x³ + 2x + 3x² + 6 — the original four terms, reordered.
Expansion is factoring's proofreader: distribute and compare term by term.

widget.prompt: Expand (x + 3)(x² + 2) to check the grouping of x³ + 3x² + 2x + 6.

commonBuilds.feedback: The constant is 3 · 2 = 6 — every term must match, and the 5 fails.
Distribute BOTH parts of (x + 3) across both parts of (x² + 2) — four products, not three.
3x² and 2x are different-degree terms — they can't merge into 5x².

widget.successFeedback: Right — x·x² + x·2 + 3·x² + 3·2, all four originals accounted for.

explanationVariants: This time the leftover quadratic DOES factor — a difference of squares.

steps.body: Pair up, pull each pair's GCF, then factor out the shared binomial.
takeaways: Grouping works exactly when both pairs expose the SAME binomial.
The leftover quadratic may factor further — or go complex (x² + k).

concept.body: Each pair gives up its own GCF first. For x³ + 4x² + 3x + 12: the first pair shares x², the second shares 3.

explanationVariants: Matching binomials mean the grouping works: (x + 4)(x² + 3).

widget.prompt: Group x³ + 4x² + 3x + 12 in pairs. What appears?

options.label: x²(x + 4) + 3(x + 4)
options.feedback: Right — a shared (x + 4), ready to factor out.

options.label: x²(x + 4) + 3(x + 3)
options.feedback: 3x + 12 = 3(x + 4) — the 12 is 3 · 4, so the binomials match.

options.label: x(x² + 4) + 3(x + 4)
options.feedback: The first pair's GCF is x² (from x³ and 4x²): x²(x + 4).

options.label: (x³ + 3x)(4x² + 12)
options.feedback: Grouping splits the SUM into two pairs — it doesn't multiply pieces together.
